preamble.summary: Targum Onkelos on Exodus shapes the narrative of redemption through consistent theological lenses: the Memra initiates and executes liberation, anti-anthropomorphism governs all theophanies (burning bush, Sinai, the cleft of the rock), and Shekinah language defines God's dwelling among Israel. The Poem of Four Nights at Exodus 12:42 is a unique targum composition linking creation, Abraham, Exodus, and Messiah.
preamble.notable_renderings: The burning bush theophany is rendered as revelation rather than appearance. The Song of the Sea celebrates the Memra. Sinai's thunder is the voice of the Memra. Moses' request to see God's glory is carefully managed — he sees the Shekinah's aftereffect, never God's face. The Poem of Four Nights (12:42) is the most distinctive Onkelos/Palestinian targum addition in the entire Torah.
preamble.theological_themes: Memra as the agent of liberation and covenant; Shekinah as God's tabernacling presence (directly connected to the Tabernacle construction); anti-anthropomorphism at every theophany; the eschatological Poem of Four Nights linking Exodus typology to Messianic expectation.

renderings.targum_text: ve'amriru yat chayehon befulchana qashya
renderings.targum_rendering: And they made their lives bitter with hard labor.
renderings.mt_rendering: They made their lives bitter with hard service.
notes: The bondage-narrative summary. Foundational for biblical Exodus theology.

renderings.hebrew_text: וַיִּשְׁמַע אֱלֹהִים אֶת־נַאֲקָתָם וַיִּזְכֹּר אֱלֹהִים אֶת־בְּרִיתוֹ
renderings.targum_text: ushtamia' qodam Adonai yat tzan'athon udekhir Adonai yat keyameih
renderings.targum_rendering: And it was heard before the LORD their groaning, and the LORD remembered his covenant.
renderings.mt_rendering: And God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant.
notes: Onkelos uses the passive 'it was heard before the LORD' rather than God actively hearing, a circumlocution that avoids implying God has ears while preserving the theological reality that Israel's cries reached heaven.

renderings.hebrew_text: וַיֵּרָא מַלְאַךְ יְהוָה אֵלָיו בְּלַבַּת־אֵשׁ מִתּוֹךְ הַסְּנֶה
renderings.targum_text: ve'itchazi leih malakha daAdonai beshalhoveita de'esha migo'o de'asna
renderings.targum_rendering: And the angel of the LORD appeared to him in a flame of fire from the midst of the bush.
renderings.mt_rendering: And the angel of the LORD appeared to him in a flame of fire from the midst of the bush.
notes: Onkelos preserves the angel as the visible agent at the burning bush, maintaining the intermediary that the Hebrew text itself provides.

renderings.targum_text: uqra leih Adonai migo'o de'asna
renderings.targum_rendering: And the LORD called to him from the midst of the bush.
renderings.mt_rendering: And God called to him from the midst of the bush.
notes: Onkelos does not insert Memra here — God's direct speech from the bush is preserved, consistent with the pattern of allowing first-person divine address.

renderings.targum_text: ana elaha de'avukh elaha de'avraham
renderings.targum_rendering: I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham.
renderings.mt_rendering: I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham.
notes: PRE-NICENE TIER S — Angel of YHWH passage. The 'angel of the LORD' (mal'akh YHWH) speaks and acts AS God across the Hebrew Bible. The Greek fathers (Justin Martyr, Dial. 56–60; Tertullian; Eusebius) read these passages as Christophanies — pre-incarnate appearances of the Son. The Targum's interpretive choices represent the Jewish counter-position. Some passages preserve the angel-as-YHWH reading; some smooth toward 'an angel sent BY YHWH.' The variation is itself the data.

MARQUEE: cited verbatim by Jesus at Matt 22:32 / Mark 12:26 / Luke 20:37 in the Sadducees' resurrection question. Jesus argues from this passage that since God is the God OF Abraham (present tense), Abraham must be alive — implying resurrection. The Targum preserves the formula precisely.

renderings.targum_text: arei Memri yehei besiyyakhah
renderings.targum_rendering: For my Memra will be in your help.
renderings.mt_rendering: For I will be with you.
notes: The promise of divine presence to Moses is mediated through the Memra, following the patriarchal pattern (Gen 28:15, 39:2). The Memra is the mode of God's accompaniment with his appointed leaders.

renderings.targum_text: Ehyeh Asher Ehyeh
renderings.targum_rendering: I Am Who I Am.
renderings.mt_rendering: I Am Who I Am.
notes: Onkelos preserves the divine name revelation without interpretation, treating it as too sacred to paraphrase. This is remarkable given Onkelos' general willingness to interpret — the Name itself is beyond targum.

renderings.hebrew_text: וַאֲנִי אֲחַזֵּק אֶת לִבּוֹ וְלֹא יְשַׁלַּח אֶת הָעָם
renderings.targum_text: va'ana atqef yat libba vela yishlach yat amma
renderings.targum_rendering: And I will strengthen his heart, and he will not let the people go.
renderings.mt_rendering: But I will harden his heart, so that he will not let the people go.
notes: The hardening-of-Pharaoh's-heart formula. Cited at Romans 9:17-18 in Paul's argument about divine sovereignty. The Targum's atqef ('strengthen') is a euphemistic alternative to the Hebrew chazaq ('harden, make strong'); rabbinic theology debates whether the hardening was punitive or causal.

renderings.targum_text: beri bukhri yisrael
renderings.targum_rendering: Israel is my firstborn son.
renderings.mt_rendering: Israel is my firstborn son.
notes: The 'Israel as firstborn son' formula. Foundational for the New Testament's typological extension to Christ as 'firstborn over all creation' (Col 1:15) and 'firstborn from the dead' (Col 1:18, Rev 1:5).

renderings.targum_text: chatan dimin attah li
renderings.targum_rendering: A bridegroom of blood are you to me.
renderings.mt_rendering: Surely you are a bridegroom of blood to me.
notes: Zipporah's mysterious circumcision episode. One of the strangest passages in the Pentateuch. Targum tracks MT.

renderings.hebrew_text: מִי יְהוָה אֲשֶׁר אֶשְׁמַע בְּקֹלוֹ לְשַׁלַּח אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵל
renderings.targum_text: לָא אִתְגְּלִי לִי שְׁמָא דַייָ דַּאֲקַבֵּיל לְמֵימְרֵיהּ לְשַׁלָּחָא יָת יִשְׂרָאֵל
renderings.targum_rendering: the name of the LORD has not been revealed to me, that I should receive his Memra to send Israel away.
renderings.mt_rendering: who is the LORD that I should obey his voice and let Israel go?
notes: Pharaoh's defiant question. Targum recasts: 'I do not know YHWH' becomes 'YHWH's name has not been revealed to me' — Pharaoh's ignorance is more politely stated, and 'voice' becomes 'Memra' as object of obedience.

renderings.hebrew_text: אֲנִי יְהוָה וָאֵרָא אֶל־אַבְרָהָם... בְּאֵל שַׁדָּי וּשְׁמִי יְהוָה לֹא נוֹדַעְתִּי לָהֶם
renderings.targum_text: ana Adonai ve'itgeleiti le'Avraham... be'El Shadday ushmei Adonai la hodeiti lehon
renderings.targum_rendering: I am the LORD. And I revealed myself to Abraham... as God Almighty, but by my name the LORD I did not make myself known to them.
renderings.mt_rendering: I am the LORD. And I appeared to Abraham... as God Almighty, but by my name the LORD I was not known to them.
notes: The theophany to the patriarchs is rendered as self-revelation (itgeleiti), and knowledge of the Name is described as God's active disclosure (hodeiti) rather than passive recognition.

renderings.targum_text: ve'appeq yatkhon mitechot fulchana demitzra'ei
renderings.targum_rendering: I will bring you out from under the burdens of Egypt.
renderings.mt_rendering: I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians.
notes: The four 'I will' deliverance promises (vv. 6-7). Foundational for the Passover seder's four-cups symbolism.

renderings.hebrew_text: אֲשֶׁר נָשָׂאתִי אֶת יָדִי לָתֵת אֹתָהּ
renderings.targum_text: diqayyemit bemeimri lemittan yatah
renderings.targum_rendering: Which I established by my Memra to give to it.
renderings.mt_rendering: Which I swore to give.
notes: PRE-NICENE TIER S: Memra-as-mediator passage. The Memra ('Word') functions as a quasi-hypostatic mediator — God acts on his behalf through his Word. This pattern across Onkelos's ~150 Memra passages forms the Jewish theological substrate from which John 1:1's Logos Christology emerges. After the post-Nicene 'Two Powers in Heaven' rabbinic polemic, Jewish theology suppressed these readings; the Targum preserves the older pre-Nicene substrate.

The land-promise oath. The Hebrew 'I lifted up my hand' (the gesture of swearing) is replaced with 'I established by my Memra' — the Memra is the divine guarantor of covenantal promise. This is theologically important: Pre-Nicene Jewish theology had a way to speak of divine self-binding through a hypostatic Word, anticipating Hebrews 6:13-18's 'God swore by himself' covenant theology.

renderings.targum_text: veyidd'un mitzra'ei arei ana Adonai
renderings.targum_rendering: And the Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD.
renderings.mt_rendering: The Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD.
notes: The 'know that I am the LORD' formula — runs through the Exodus narrative as the goal of the plagues. Foundational for biblical knowledge-of-God theology.

renderings.targum_text: אֲרֵי לֵית כַּייָ אֱלָהֲנָא
renderings.targum_rendering: there is none like the LORD our God.
renderings.mt_rendering: that you may know that there is no one like the LORD our God.
notes: Moses to Pharaoh re: frogs. Strict monotheism affirmation preserved — even mid-plague, the theological assertion holds.

renderings.targum_text: וּבְדִיל לְאִשְׁתָּעָאָה שְׁמִי בְּכָל אַרְעָא
renderings.targum_rendering: in order that my name might be declared throughout all the earth.
renderings.mt_rendering: in order that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth.
notes: YHWH to Pharaoh through Moses. Cited Romans 9:17 — Paul's election theology rests on this verse. Divine purpose for Pharaoh's resistance is the public declaration of YHWH's name.

renderings.targum_text: וּבְדִיל דִּתְשַׁעֵי קֳדָם בְּרָךְ וּבַר בְּרָךְ
renderings.targum_rendering: in order that you may recount before your son and your son's son.
renderings.mt_rendering: and that you may tell in the hearing of your son and of your grandson.
notes: Locust-plague pedagogical purpose. 'In your son's hearing' → 'before your son' — anti-anthropomorphism applied even to inter-human storytelling. The plagues are the foundation of the Pesach-recital tradition.

renderings.hebrew_text: אֲשֶׁר יַפְלֶה יְהוָה בֵּין מִצְרַיִם וּבֵין יִשְׂרָאֵל
renderings.targum_text: deyafresh Adonai bein mitzra'ei uvein yisrael
renderings.targum_rendering: That the LORD distinguishes between Egypt and Israel.
renderings.mt_rendering: That the LORD makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel.
notes: The distinction-between-Egypt-and-Israel formula. Foundational for biblical election theology.

renderings.targum_text: ve'itgelei be'ar'a deMitzrayim... ana Adonai
renderings.targum_rendering: And I will reveal myself in the land of Egypt... I am the LORD.
renderings.mt_rendering: And I will pass through the land of Egypt... I am the LORD.
notes: God does not 'pass through' Egypt like a traveler. Onkelos replaces physical movement with divine self-revelation, consistent with the theology that God acts without spatial displacement.

renderings.targum_text: ve'echzei yat dema ve'echush aleikhon
renderings.targum_rendering: And I will see the blood and I will have mercy upon you.
renderings.mt_rendering: And I will see the blood and I will pass over you.
notes: Onkelos interprets 'pass over' (pasach) as 'have mercy' (echush), shifting from a physical action (skipping over houses) to a theological one (exercising mercy). This deepens the Passover from spatial movement to divine compassion.

renderings.targum_text: vihei yoma haden lekhon ledukhran
renderings.targum_rendering: And this day shall be a memorial to you.
renderings.mt_rendering: This day shall be for you a memorial day.
notes: The Passover-memorial command. Echoed at Luke 22:19 / 1 Cor 11:24-25 ('do this in remembrance of me') — the Christian Eucharist as Passover-memorial extension.

renderings.targum_text: vela yitten malakha demachei le'me'al levatekhon
renderings.targum_rendering: And he will not allow the destroying angel to enter your houses.
renderings.mt_rendering: And he will not allow the destroyer to enter your houses.
notes: The 'destroyer' (mashchit) is identified as 'the destroying angel' (malakha demachei), an angelic agent rather than an impersonal force. This clarifies the agent of the plague while distancing God from direct destruction.

renderings.targum_text: leilya denetira hu qodam Adonai... arba'a leilavvan
renderings.targum_rendering: It is a night of watching before the LORD... four nights [are recorded in the memorial book].
renderings.mt_rendering: It was a night of watching for the LORD.
notes: This is the Poem of Four Nights, the most famous unique composition in the targum tradition. Onkelos (and more fully Pseudo-Jonathan and Neofiti) expands this verse into a cosmic four-night schema: (1) the night of creation when God's Memra illuminated the darkness, (2) the night of Abraham's covenant/Aqedah, (3) the night of the Exodus, and (4) the night of the Messiah's coming. This links all of salvation history into a single nocturnal typology.

renderings.targum_text: vekhol arel la yeikhul beih
renderings.targum_rendering: And no uncircumcised man shall eat of it.
renderings.mt_rendering: But no uncircumcised person shall eat of it.
notes: The Passover circumcision-requirement. Establishes that Passover participation is bound to covenant inclusion. Echoes through 1 Cor 5:7-8 ('Christ our Passover... let us keep the feast').

renderings.targum_text: aqdesh qodamai kol bukhra
renderings.targum_rendering: Sanctify before me every firstborn.
renderings.mt_rendering: Consecrate to me all the firstborn.
notes: The firstborn-redemption command. Cited at Luke 2:23 in the presentation of Jesus at the temple. Foundational for the Jewish pidyon ha-ben (firstborn-redemption) ritual and the Christian theology of Christ as the firstborn redeemer.

renderings.hebrew_text: וְהָיָה לְךָ לְאוֹת עַל יָדְכָה וּלְזִכָּרוֹן בֵּין עֵינֶיךָ
renderings.targum_text: vihei lakh le'at al yedekh ul'idkar bein einakh
renderings.targum_rendering: And it shall be for you a sign on your hand and a memorial between your eyes.
renderings.mt_rendering: And it shall be to you as a sign on your hand and as a memorial between your eyes.
notes: Foundational text for the tefillin (phylacteries) tradition.

renderings.hebrew_text: וַיהוָה הֹלֵךְ לִפְנֵיהֶם יוֹמָם בְּעַמּוּד עָנָן
renderings.targum_text: vaAdonai madbar qodamehon bimama be'amuda da'anana
renderings.targum_rendering: And the LORD was leading before them by day in a pillar of cloud.
renderings.mt_rendering: And the LORD was going before them by day in a pillar of cloud.
notes: 'Going' (holekh) becomes 'leading' (madbar), shifting from physical locomotion to purposeful guidance. God does not walk but directs.

renderings.targum_text: tit'attadu vechazu yat purqana deAdonai
renderings.targum_rendering: Stand still and see the salvation of the LORD.
renderings.mt_rendering: Stand firm, and see the salvation of the LORD.
notes: The classic stand-still-see-salvation formula. Foundational for biblical theology of divine intervention.

renderings.hebrew_text: וַיִּסַּע מַלְאַךְ הָאֱלֹהִים הַהֹלֵךְ לִפְנֵי מַחֲנֵה יִשְׂרָאֵל וַיֵּלֶךְ מֵאַחֲרֵיהֶם
renderings.targum_text: וּנְטַל מַלְאֲכָא דַייָ דִּמְהַלֵּךְ קֳדָם מַשְׁרִיתָא דְיִשְׂרָאֵל וַאֲזַל מִבָּתְרֵיהוֹן
renderings.targum_rendering: the angel of the LORD who was going before the camp of Israel moved and went behind them.
renderings.mt_rendering: the angel of God who was going before the host of Israel moved and went behind them.
notes: Pre-Nicene Tier S. The Red Sea theophany — the angel of YHWH and the pillar of cloud act in concert as divine military protection. Cited 1 Cor 10:1-4 (Paul: 'all were under the cloud') as typological-baptism.

renderings.hebrew_text: וַיּוֹלֶךְ יְהוָה אֶת הַיָּם בְּרוּחַ קָדִים עַזָּה
renderings.targum_text: ve'ovil Adonai yat yamma beruach qiddum taqqifa
renderings.targum_rendering: And the LORD led the sea with a strong east wind.
renderings.mt_rendering: And the LORD drove the sea back by a strong east wind.
notes: The Red Sea crossing. Foundational for OT exodus-typology and for Christian baptismal typology (1 Cor 10:1-2).

renderings.hebrew_text: וַיַּרְא יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶת־הַיָּד הַגְּדֹלָה אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה יְהוָה בְּמִצְרַיִם
renderings.targum_text: vachaza Yisrael yat gevurta rabbeta da'avad Adonai beMitzrayim
renderings.targum_rendering: And Israel saw the great power which the LORD had wrought in Egypt.
renderings.mt_rendering: And Israel saw the great hand which the LORD had wielded against Egypt.
notes: 'The great hand' becomes 'the great power' (gevurta rabbeta), removing the anthropomorphic image of God's hand and replacing it with an abstract attribute.

renderings.hebrew_text: אָז יָשִׁיר־מֹשֶׁה וּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶת־הַשִּׁירָה הַזֹּאת לַיהוָה
renderings.targum_text: bedain shabbach Mosheh uvenei Yisrael yat tushbechta hada qodam Adonai
renderings.targum_rendering: Then Moses and the children of Israel sang this song of praise before the LORD.
renderings.mt_rendering: Then Moses and the children of Israel sang this song to the LORD.
notes: The Song of the Sea is described as praise (tushbechta) offered 'before the LORD' (qodam Adonai), aligning the Exodus celebration with synagogue worship patterns.

renderings.targum_text: tushbechti vetiqfi Adonai vahava li lefurqan
renderings.targum_rendering: My praise and my strength is the LORD, and he has become for me redemption.
renderings.mt_rendering: The LORD is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation.
notes: Salvation (yeshu'ah) is rendered as redemption (furqan), the same Aramaic term used in messianic contexts, linking the Exodus redemption typologically to eschatological deliverance.

renderings.targum_text: Adonai gevur qaravayya Adonai shemeih
renderings.targum_rendering: The LORD is a warrior in battle; the LORD is his name.
renderings.mt_rendering: The LORD is a man of war; the LORD is his name.
notes: 'Man of war' (ish milchamah) becomes 'warrior in battle' (gevur qaravayya), removing the word 'man' (ish) from any description of God while preserving the martial imagery.

renderings.targum_text: yeminakh Adonai meshabbachta becheilah
renderings.targum_rendering: Your right hand, O LORD, is glorious in power.
renderings.mt_rendering: Your right hand, O LORD, is glorious in power.
notes: Onkelos preserves 'right hand' in the poetic Song of the Sea, treating it as established liturgical language. The targum tradition is more tolerant of anthropomorphism in poetry than in narrative.

renderings.hebrew_text: מִי־כָמֹכָה בָּאֵלִם יְהוָה מִי כָּמֹכָה נֶאְדָּר בַּקֹּדֶשׁ
renderings.targum_text: לֵית בַּר מִנָּךְ אַתְּ הוּא אֱלָהָא יְיָ לֵית בַּר מִנָּךְ אַדִּיר בְּקוּדְשָׁא
renderings.targum_rendering: there is none beside you — you are God, O LORD! There is none beside you, glorious in holiness.
renderings.mt_rendering: who is like you, O LORD, among the gods? Who is like you, majestic in holiness?
notes: Song of the Sea. Hebrew 'gods' (אֵלִם) softened to monotheistic affirmation: 'there is none beside you.' Standard Targum handling — strict monotheism at every textually-permissible point.

renderings.hebrew_text: הִנְנִי מַמְטִיר לָכֶם לֶחֶם מִן הַשָּׁמָיִם
renderings.targum_text: ha ana machet lekhon lachma min shemayya
renderings.targum_rendering: Behold, I will rain bread for you from the heavens.
renderings.mt_rendering: Behold, I am going to rain bread from heaven for you.
notes: The manna-from-heaven promise. Cited at John 6:31 ('he gave them bread from heaven to eat') in Jesus' bread-of-life discourse. The Targum's literal preservation matches the form Jesus quotes.

renderings.hebrew_text: וַיִּקְרְאוּ בֵית יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶת שְׁמוֹ מָן
renderings.targum_text: uqro veit yisrael yat shemei manna
renderings.targum_rendering: And the house of Israel called its name 'manna.'
renderings.mt_rendering: And the house of Israel called its name 'manna.'
notes: The naming of manna. Cited extensively at John 6 in Jesus' Bread of Life discourse, and at Heb 9:4 (the golden urn of manna in the ark).

renderings.hebrew_text: הִנְנִי עֹמֵד לְפָנֶיךָ שָּׁם עַל הַצּוּר בְּחֹרֵב וְהִכִּיתָ בַצּוּר וְיָצְאוּ מִמֶּנּוּ מַיִם
renderings.targum_text: ha ana qa'em qodamakh tamman al kefa bechorev vetimchei bekhefa veyippeqan minneih mayya
renderings.targum_rendering: Behold, I will be standing before you there on the rock at Horeb, and you shall strike the rock, and water shall flow out from it.
renderings.mt_rendering: Behold, I will stand before you there on the rock at Horeb, and you shall strike the rock, and water shall come out of it.
notes: MARQUEE: cited at 1 Corinthians 10:4 ('they drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them, and the Rock was Christ'). Paul develops the rabbinic legend of the well-of-Miriam — that the rock followed Israel through the wilderness — into a Christological allegory. The Targum preserves the literal episode.

renderings.hebrew_text: וְהָיָה כַּאֲשֶׁר יָרִים מֹשֶׁה יָדוֹ וְגָבַר יִשְׂרָאֵל
renderings.targum_text: vahava kad arim moshe yadohi mit'gabber yisrael
renderings.targum_rendering: When Moses lifted up his hands, Israel prevailed.
renderings.mt_rendering: Whenever Moses held up his hand, Israel prevailed.
notes: The Amalek-battle prayer. Foundational for biblical theology of intercessory prayer affecting historical outcomes.

renderings.hebrew_text: כִּי־יָד עַל־כֵּס יָהּ מִלְחָמָה לַיהוָה בַּעֲמָלֵק
renderings.targum_text: arei bishevuah min qodam kurseih deyeqara daAdonai qerav laAdonai ba'Amaleq
renderings.targum_rendering: For by an oath from before the throne of the glory of the LORD, the LORD will wage war against Amalek.
renderings.mt_rendering: For a hand upon the throne of the LORD — war for the LORD against Amalek.
notes: The cryptic 'hand upon the throne of Yah' is interpreted as a solemn oath from before God's glorious throne. Onkelos transforms a physical gesture into a juridical act, and introduces the 'glory' (yeqar) as a buffer for direct reference to God's throne.

renderings.hebrew_text: עַתָּה יָדַעְתִּי כִּי גָדוֹל יְהוָה מִכָּל הָאֱלֹהִים
renderings.targum_text: kean yaddait arei rav Adonai mikol elahin
renderings.targum_rendering: Now I know that the LORD is greater than all gods.
renderings.mt_rendering: Now I know that the LORD is greater than all gods.
notes: Jethro's confession. Foundational for the OT 'gods' / 'God' distinction. Echoes the Egyptian-magicians' 'this is the finger of God' (Exod 8:19).

renderings.hebrew_text: וּמֹשֶׁה עָלָה אֶל־הָאֱלֹהִים וַיִּקְרָא אֵלָיו יְהוָה מִן־הָהָר
renderings.targum_text: uMosheh seliq leqodam Adonai uqra leih Adonai min tura
renderings.targum_rendering: And Moses went up before the LORD, and the LORD called to him from the mountain.
renderings.mt_rendering: And Moses went up to God, and the LORD called to him from the mountain.
notes: Moses goes up 'before the LORD' (leqodam Adonai) rather than 'to God,' using the reverential circumlocution that avoids implying God is spatially located on the mountain.

renderings.targum_text: utehevon qodamai chavviva mikkol amemmayya
renderings.targum_rendering: And you shall be precious before me from among all the peoples.
renderings.mt_rendering: And you shall be my treasured possession out of all the peoples.
notes: The covenant-treasure formula (segullah). Cited at Titus 2:14 and 1 Pet 2:9 (laos eis peripoieisin) as the Christian-people identification. The Targum's chavviva ('precious, beloved') captures the affective sense of segullah.

renderings.hebrew_text: וְאַתֶּם תִּהְיוּ לִי מַמְלֶכֶת כֹּהֲנִים וְגוֹי קָדוֹשׁ
renderings.targum_text: ve'atton tehevon qodamai malkhin kahanin ve'amma qaddisha
renderings.targum_rendering: And you shall be before me kings, priests, and a holy people.
renderings.mt_rendering: You shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.
notes: MARQUEE: cited at 1 Peter 2:9 ('you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession') and Revelation 1:6, 5:10. The Targum's expansion to malkhin kahanin ('kings, priests') anticipates the rabbinic reading of Israel-as-collective-royalty-and-priesthood.

renderings.hebrew_text: הִנֵּה אָנֹכִי בָּא אֵלֶיךָ בְּעַב הֶעָנָן
renderings.targum_text: ha ana mit'gle alakh be'iv anana
renderings.targum_rendering: Behold, I shall be revealed to you in the thick cloud.
renderings.mt_rendering: Behold, I am coming to you in a thick cloud.
notes: The Sinai-cloud-theophany announcement. Foundational for biblical cloud-Shekinah theology.

renderings.hebrew_text: וַיּוֹצֵא מֹשֶׁה אֶת־הָעָם לִקְרַאת הָאֱלֹהִים מִן־הַמַּחֲנֶה
renderings.targum_text: ve'appeiq Mosheh yat amma le'araa shekhinteih daAdonai min mashrita
renderings.targum_rendering: And Moses brought out the people to meet the Shekinah of the LORD from the camp.
renderings.mt_rendering: And Moses brought the people out to meet God from the camp.
notes: Israel does not meet God directly but the Shekinah of the LORD. This is one of the most significant Shekinah passages in Onkelos — the Sinai theophany is an encounter with God's indwelling presence, not God's essence.

renderings.hebrew_text: מִפְּנֵי אֲשֶׁר יָרַד עָלָיו יְהוָה בָּאֵשׁ
renderings.targum_text: min qodam de'itgeli aloi Adonai be'esha
renderings.targum_rendering: Because the LORD revealed himself upon it in fire.
renderings.mt_rendering: Because the LORD descended upon it in fire.
notes: God does not 'descend' upon Sinai. The descent is replaced with revelation (itgeli), preserving divine transcendence even at the most dramatic theophany in the Torah.

renderings.targum_text: ve'itgeli Adonai al tura deSinai
renderings.targum_rendering: And the LORD revealed himself upon Mount Sinai.
renderings.mt_rendering: And the LORD came down upon Mount Sinai.
notes: Repeated rendering: every instance of divine descent at Sinai is transformed into divine revelation. Onkelos is systematic and consistent in this substitution.

renderings.targum_text: umalil Adonai yat kol pitgamayya ha'ilein
renderings.targum_rendering: And the LORD spoke all these words.
renderings.mt_rendering: And God spoke all these words.
notes: At the giving of the Ten Commandments, Onkelos uses 'the LORD' rather than Elohim, emphasizing that the covenant God of Israel (YHWH) — not a generic deity — delivers the commandments.

renderings.hebrew_text: לֹא תִשָּׂא אֶת שֵׁם יְהוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ לַשָּׁוְא
renderings.targum_text: la teimei beshema deAdonai elahakh lemaggana
renderings.targum_rendering: You shall not swear by the name of the LORD your God in vain.
renderings.mt_rendering: You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain.
notes: PRE-NICENE TIER S: Memra-as-mediator passage. The Memra ('Word') functions as a quasi-hypostatic mediator — God acts on his behalf through his Word. This pattern across Onkelos's ~150 Memra passages forms the Jewish theological substrate from which John 1:1's Logos Christology emerges. After the post-Nicene 'Two Powers in Heaven' rabbinic polemic, Jewish theology suppressed these readings; the Targum preserves the older pre-Nicene substrate.

The third commandment. Onkelos interprets 'taking the name in vain' as 'swearing in the name in vain' — narrowing the scope to the false-oath sense. This interpretive choice shapes the rabbinic understanding of the commandment as primarily about oath-keeping.

renderings.targum_text: arei shitta yomin avad Adonai
renderings.targum_rendering: For in six days the LORD made.
renderings.mt_rendering: For in six days the LORD made.
notes: The Sabbath creation-rationale (the Exodus version, expanded vs Deut 5's Egypt-deliverance rationale). DSS 4QDeutⁿ harmonizes by combining BOTH rationales.

renderings.targum_text: vekhol amma chazin yat qalayya
renderings.targum_rendering: And all the people were seeing the thunderings.
renderings.mt_rendering: And all the people were seeing the thunderings.
notes: Onkelos preserves the synesthetic 'seeing the thunderings,' which rabbinic tradition interprets as the people seeing the voice of God — each commandment emerging as visible fire.

renderings.hebrew_text: וַיַּעַמְדוּ מֵרָחֹק... וְאַל־יְדַבֵּר עִמָּנוּ אֱלֹהִים פֶּן־נָמוּת
renderings.targum_text: veqamu merachiq... vela yitmalal immana min qodam Adonai dilma nemut
renderings.targum_rendering: And they stood afar off... and let not [a word] be spoken with us from before the LORD, lest we die.
renderings.mt_rendering: And they stood afar off... and let not God speak with us, lest we die.
notes: The people's fear of God speaking directly is rendered as fear of speech 'from before the LORD,' adding the reverential circumlocution even in the people's own words.

renderings.hebrew_text: עַיִן תַּחַת עַיִן שֵׁן תַּחַת שֵׁן
renderings.targum_text: ein chalaf ein shin chalaf shin
renderings.targum_rendering: Eye for eye, tooth for tooth.
renderings.mt_rendering: Eye for eye, tooth for tooth.
notes: The lex talionis. Cited (and reframed) by Jesus at Matt 5:38-39 ('you have heard that it was said: an eye for an eye... but I say to you, do not resist the one who is evil').

renderings.hebrew_text: אֱלֹהִים לֹא תְקַלֵּל וְנָשִׂיא בְעַמְּךָ לֹא תָאֹר
renderings.targum_text: דַיָּנָא לָא תְקַלֵּל וְרַבָּא בְעַמָּךְ לָא תְלוּט
renderings.targum_rendering: you shall not curse the judge, nor curse the ruler of your people.
renderings.mt_rendering: you shall not revile God, nor curse a ruler of your people.
notes: Targum interprets אֱלֹהִים here as 'judge' (דַיָּנָא) — the rabbinic understanding that this verse protects human authorities, not (as Acts 23:5 cites) God's high priest. Cited Acts 23:5 (Paul before the council).

renderings.targum_text: la teikhul besra bachalva
renderings.targum_rendering: You shall not eat meat in milk.
renderings.mt_rendering: You shall not boil a young goat in its mother's milk.
notes: The kid-in-mother's-milk law — foundational for the Jewish kosher prohibition on mixing meat and dairy. The Targum's interpretive expansion ('you shall not eat meat in milk') makes the rabbinic application explicit.

renderings.targum_text: ha ana shaleach malakha qodamakh
renderings.targum_rendering: Behold, I am sending an angel before you.
renderings.mt_rendering: Behold, I send an angel before you.
notes: The angel-of-the-LORD passage. Onkelos preserves malakha ('angel') against speculative identifications. Christian tradition reads the malakha across the OT as Christophanies; the Jewish reading sees a created angel.

renderings.targum_text: ha dam qeyama
renderings.targum_rendering: Behold, the blood of the covenant.
renderings.mt_rendering: Behold the blood of the covenant.
notes: MARQUEE — cited verbatim by Jesus at Matt 26:28 / Mark 14:24 / Luke 22:20 in the institution of the Eucharist ('this is my blood of the covenant'). Foundational for Christian Eucharistic theology.

renderings.targum_text: vechazo yat yeqara de'Elaha deYisrael
renderings.targum_rendering: And they saw the glory of the God of Israel.
renderings.mt_rendering: And they saw the God of Israel.
notes: This is one of the most critical anti-anthropomorphic moves in all of Onkelos. The elders cannot have 'seen God' — they saw 'the glory (yeqar) of the God of Israel.' No human sees God directly; they see the kavod/yeqar.

renderings.targum_text: vechazo yat yeqara daAdonai vechadiu be'qorbanehon de'itqabilu keilu akhalu veshatiu
renderings.targum_rendering: And they saw the glory of the LORD, and they rejoiced in their offerings which were accepted as though they ate and drank.
renderings.mt_rendering: And they beheld God, and they ate and drank.
notes: Onkelos cannot allow the casual statement that the elders saw God and then had a meal. The seeing is redirected to God's glory, and the eating/drinking is reinterpreted as joy over accepted sacrifices — transforming a covenant meal into a liturgical celebration.

renderings.targum_text: veya'avdun qodomi maqdasha ve'ashrei Shekhineti beineihon
renderings.targum_rendering: And let them make before me a sanctuary, and I will cause my Shekinah to dwell among them.
renderings.mt_rendering: And let them make me a sanctuary, and I will dwell among them.
notes: The foundational Tabernacle verse: God does not dwell among Israel directly but causes his Shekinah to dwell among them. This establishes the Shekinah as the mode of divine indwelling in sacred space — the theological heart of the Tabernacle.

renderings.targum_text: ve'azammen lakh tamman memreih
renderings.targum_rendering: And I will appoint my Memra to meet you there.
renderings.mt_rendering: There I will meet with you.
notes: Pre-Nicene Tier S — the Memra meets-with-Moses at the mercy-seat. Foundational for OT atonement-encounter theology. The mercy-seat (kapporet) becomes the Greek hilastērion at Romans 3:25 — Paul's title for Christ.

renderings.hebrew_text: וְהִבְדִּילָה הַפָּרֹכֶת לָכֶם בֵּין הַקֹּדֶשׁ וּבֵין קֹדֶשׁ הַקֳּדָשִׁים
renderings.targum_text: וְתַפְרֵישׁ פָּרוֹכְתָּא לְכוֹן בֵּין קוּדְשָׁא וּבֵין קוֹדֶשׁ קוּדְשַׁיָּא
renderings.targum_rendering: the curtain shall divide for you between the holy place and the most holy place.
renderings.mt_rendering: the curtain shall separate for you the holy place from the most holy place.
notes: Tabernacle veil instruction. Literal preservation — the architecture of holiness is preserved exactly because the Holy of Holies is where the Shekinah dwells.

renderings.targum_text: וְתִתֵּן בְּחֹשֶׁן דִּינָא יָת אוּרִים וְיָת תּוּמִּים
renderings.targum_rendering: you shall put into the breastpiece of judgment the Urim and the Thummim.
renderings.mt_rendering: you shall put in the breastpiece of judgment the Urim and the Thummim.
notes: Urim and Thummim instruction. The priestly-divination instruments preserved by name — these are the sole sanctioned means of seeking divine guidance. Pre-Nicene relevance: institutional mediation of divine will.

renderings.hebrew_text: וְשָׁכַנְתִּי בְּתוֹךְ בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְהָיִיתִי לָהֶם לֵאלֹהִים
renderings.targum_text: ve'ashrei Shekhineti bego benei Yisrael ve'ehei lehon l'Elah
renderings.targum_rendering: And I will cause my Shekinah to dwell among the children of Israel, and I will be their God.
renderings.mt_rendering: And I will dwell among the children of Israel and will be their God.
notes: Repeated Shekinah formula: God's indwelling is consistently expressed through the Shekinah. The covenant formula 'I will be their God' is preserved without mediation — the relationship is direct even if the mode of presence is the Shekinah.

renderings.hebrew_text: וְיָדְעוּ כִּי אֲנִי יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵיהֶם אֲשֶׁר הוֹצֵאתִי אֹתָם מֵאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם לְשָׁכְנִי בְתוֹכָם
renderings.targum_text: viyeid'un arei ana Adonai Elahehon de'appiqit yathon me'ar'a deMitzrayim le'ashraah Shekhineti beineihon
renderings.targum_rendering: And they shall know that I am the LORD their God, who brought them out from the land of Egypt, to cause my Shekinah to dwell among them.
renderings.mt_rendering: And they shall know that I am the LORD their God, who brought them out of the land of Egypt, that I might dwell among them.
notes: The purpose of the Exodus is Shekinah-dwelling. Onkelos ties liberation directly to divine presence: God freed Israel so that his Shekinah could tabernacle in their midst.

renderings.hebrew_text: לִפְנֵי הַכַּפֹּרֶת אֲשֶׁר עַל־הָעֵדֻת אֲשֶׁר אִוָּעֵד לְךָ שָׁמָּה
renderings.targum_text: קֳדָם כַּפּוּרְתָּא דִי עַל סָהֲדוּתָא דַּאֲזַמֵּן מֵימְרִי לָךְ תַמָּן
renderings.targum_rendering: before the mercy seat that is upon the Testimony, where I will appoint my Memra to you.
renderings.mt_rendering: before the mercy seat that is over the Testimony, where I will meet with you.
notes: Incense altar instruction. The 'meeting place' between God and Moses is recast as 'where my Memra will be appointed for you' — divine encounter mediated through the Word, not direct presence.

renderings.targum_text: arei ata hi bein Memri uveineikhon
renderings.targum_rendering: For it is a sign between my Memra and you.
renderings.mt_rendering: For it is a sign between me and you.
notes: The Sabbath sign, like the rainbow sign (Gen 9:12), is placed between the Memra and Israel rather than between God directly and Israel. Covenant signs are mediated through the Word.

renderings.targum_text: beyoma shevi'a'ah shevat venach
renderings.targum_rendering: On the seventh day he ceased and rested.
renderings.mt_rendering: On the seventh day he ceased and was refreshed.
notes: The Hebrew vayinnafash ('was refreshed,' from nefesh/soul) is softened to 'rested' (nach), removing any implication that God needed refreshment or has a soul that required restoration.

renderings.targum_text: ukh'an sh'voq min qodamai viyitqaf rug'zi behon
renderings.targum_rendering: And now, desist from before me, and let my anger be strong against them.
renderings.mt_rendering: Now therefore let me alone, that my anger may burn against them.
notes: 'Let me alone' becomes 'desist from before me,' and 'anger burning' becomes 'anger being strong' (yitqaf) — Onkelos subtly adjusts the metaphors to reduce the anthropomorphic intensity while preserving the drama of the Golden Calf crisis.

renderings.hebrew_text: וַיִּנָּחֶם יְהוָה עַל־הָרָעָה אֲשֶׁר דִּבֶּר לַעֲשׂוֹת לְעַמּוֹ
renderings.targum_text: vetav qodam Adonai al bishta di malil leme'bad le'ammeih
renderings.targum_rendering: And it was good before the LORD concerning the evil which he had spoken to do to his people.
renderings.mt_rendering: And the LORD relented concerning the evil which he had spoken of doing to his people.
notes: God does not 'relent' or 'change his mind' in Onkelos. The anthropopathic verb nacham is replaced with 'it was good before the LORD,' a reverential formula that preserves divine immutability.

renderings.targum_text: luchei ketivin mittarin trein ittarehon
renderings.targum_rendering: Tablets written on both their sides.
renderings.mt_rendering: Tablets that were written on both sides.
notes: The double-sided Decalogue tablets. Rabbinic tradition (b. Shabbat 104a) reads this as miraculous engraving.

renderings.hebrew_text: וְעַתָּה אִם תִּשָּׂא חַטָּאתָם וְאִם אַיִן מְחֵנִי נָא מִסִּפְרְךָ אֲשֶׁר כָּתָבְתָּ
renderings.targum_text: ukhe'an im shevoq lechovehon ve'im la machei na yati misifrakh dikhtavt
renderings.targum_rendering: Now if you will forgive their sin... but if not, blot me, I pray, from your book that you have written.
renderings.mt_rendering: But now, if you will forgive their sin... but if not, please blot me out of your book that you have written.
notes: Moses' intercessory offer of substitution. Echoed at Romans 9:3 ('I could wish that I myself were accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers'). The 'book' becomes the eschatological Book of Life (Phil 4:3, Rev 3:5, 13:8, 20:12, 21:27).

renderings.hebrew_text: וְדִבֶּר יְהוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה פָּנִים אֶל פָּנִים
renderings.targum_text: umallel Adonai im moshe mamlel im mamlel
renderings.targum_rendering: And the LORD spoke with Moses speech with speech.
renderings.mt_rendering: The LORD would speak to Moses face to face.
notes: The intimate 'face to face' is replaced with mamlel im mamlel ('speech with speech'), avoiding the anthropomorphic claim of seeing God's face. The rabbinic tradition reconciles this with Numbers 12:8 ('mouth to mouth') by interpreting both as direct prophetic communication, not visual encounter.

renderings.targum_text: Shekhineti tehakh ve'anikha lakh
renderings.targum_rendering: My Shekinah shall go, and I will give you rest.
renderings.mt_rendering: My presence shall go, and I will give you rest.
notes: 'My face' (panai, literally 'my faces') is rendered 'my Shekinah.' God's face — the most intimate anthropomorphism — becomes the Shekinah, the divine presence that accompanies Israel without compromising God's transcendence.

renderings.targum_text: achzini kean yat yeqarakh
renderings.targum_rendering: Show me, I pray, your Glory.
renderings.mt_rendering: Please show me your glory.
notes: MARQUEE — Moses' request to see God's Glory. The Targum's yeqarakh ('your Glory') matches MT's kavod. v. 19 specifies that what Moses sees is God's GOODNESS, not God himself; v. 20 explicitly says 'no human shall see me and live.' Foundational for the Christian distinction between vision-of-essence and vision-of-glory (developed in Eastern Orthodox theology of theosis).

renderings.hebrew_text: לֹא תוּכַל לִרְאֹת אֶת־פָּנָי כִּי לֹא־יִרְאַנִי הָאָדָם וָחָי
renderings.targum_text: la tikdar lemechzei yat appai arei la yechzinnani enasha veyeqayyam
renderings.targum_rendering: You are not able to see my face, for no man shall see me and live.
renderings.mt_rendering: You cannot see my face, for no man shall see me and live.
notes: Remarkably, Onkelos preserves 'my face' here rather than substituting Shekinah or glory. The point is prohibition: no one can see God's face. The literal rendering reinforces the impossibility of direct vision of God, which is the very principle that drives Onkelos' anti-anthropomorphism everywhere else.

renderings.targum_text: vetechzei yat di vatrai ve'appai la yitchazun
renderings.targum_rendering: And you shall see what is behind me, but my face shall not be seen.
renderings.mt_rendering: And you shall see my back, but my face shall not be seen.
notes: 'My back' becomes 'what is behind me' (di vatrai), subtly shifting from a body part to a spatial/temporal concept — what follows after God's passing, not God's physical backside.

renderings.targum_text: ve'itgeli Adonai be'anana
renderings.targum_rendering: And the LORD revealed himself in the cloud.
renderings.mt_rendering: And the LORD descended in the cloud.
notes: God does not descend into the cloud but reveals himself in it. The cloud remains the medium of theophany, but divine movement is replaced with self-disclosure.

renderings.targum_text: Adonai Adonai Elaha rachama vechanina
renderings.targum_rendering: The LORD, the LORD, God compassionate and gracious.
renderings.mt_rendering: The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious.
notes: The Thirteen Attributes of Mercy are rendered with minimal change. Onkelos treats this divine self-description as authoritative and does not adjust the attributive language — these qualities describe God's character, not his body.

renderings.targum_text: tehakh ke'an Shekhinteih daAdonai begavvana
renderings.targum_rendering: Let the Shekinah of the LORD go now in our midst.
renderings.mt_rendering: Let the Lord go in our midst.
notes: Moses' plea for God's presence is a plea for the Shekinah. God does not 'go' in Israel's midst — the Shekinah does. This is one of the clearest Shekinah passages in Exodus.

renderings.hebrew_text: כִּי קָרַן עוֹר פָּנָיו בְּדַבְּרוֹ אִתּוֹ
renderings.targum_text: arei sagi yeqar mishekh apohi bememaleluteih imei
renderings.targum_rendering: For the splendor of his face was great as he spoke with him.
renderings.mt_rendering: The skin of his face shone because he had been talking with God.
notes: Moses' shining face. The Targum interprets karan ('horned/shone') as 'splendor.' Cited at 2 Cor 3:7-18 by Paul in his glory-of-Moses-vs-glory-of-Christ contrast.

renderings.hebrew_text: וַיְמַלֵּא אֹתוֹ רוּחַ אֱלֹהִים בְּחָכְמָה בִּתְבוּנָה
renderings.targum_text: וְאַשְׁלֵים עֲלוֹהִי רוּחָא דִנְבוּאָה מִן קֳדָם יְיָ בְּחֻכְמְתָא בְסוּכְלְתָנוּ
renderings.targum_rendering: the spirit of prophecy from before the LORD filled him with wisdom and understanding.
renderings.mt_rendering: and he has filled him with the Spirit of God, with skill, with intelligence.
notes: Bezalel's gifting for the tabernacle. Even craft-skill is 'spirit of prophecy from before the LORD' — anti-anthropomorphism: God doesn't directly fill, the Spirit comes from his presence.

renderings.targum_text: va'avad betzaltzel yat arona
renderings.targum_rendering: And Bezalel made the ark.
renderings.mt_rendering: Bezalel made the ark.
notes: The Spirit-filled craftsman Bezalel. Foundational for biblical theology of artistic vocation as Spirit-gift.

renderings.hebrew_text: וַיְכַס הֶעָנָן אֶת־אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד וּכְבוֹד יְהוָה מָלֵא אֶת־הַמִּשְׁכָּן
renderings.targum_text: vekhassa anana yat mashkan ziman viyeqara daAdonai malei yat mishkena
renderings.targum_rendering: And the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of the LORD filled the Tabernacle.
renderings.mt_rendering: And the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of the LORD filled the Tabernacle.
notes: At the climax of Exodus, Onkelos renders 'glory' (kavod/yeqar) literally. The glory filling the Tabernacle is the culmination of the Shekinah theology developed throughout the book — God's presence has come to dwell among his people.

renderings.hebrew_text: וְלֹא־יָכֹל מֹשֶׁה לָבוֹא אֶל־אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד כִּי־שָׁכַן עָלָיו הֶעָנָן
renderings.targum_text: vela yakhil Mosheh le'me'al lemashkan zimna arei sherat aloi anana
renderings.targum_rendering: And Moses was not able to enter the tent of meeting, because the cloud had settled upon it.
renderings.mt_rendering: And Moses was not able to enter the tent of meeting, because the cloud had settled upon it.
notes: The verb sherat ('settled/rested') replaces shakhan ('dwelt'), using a term that emphasizes the cloud's tangible presence. The Shekinah is so powerfully manifest that even Moses cannot enter.
